wholeness that emerges in some of the literature on the anthropology of one religious tradition or another with such traditions sometimes represented as deriving from self-contained theologies, or reduced to a demotic, almost spontaneous religiosity. for several years now, there has been considerable academic attention focused on ethics and so-called piety movements associated with what has been dubbed the islamic awakening (arabic, sahwa) in various places in the middle east, and particularly in egypt. this attention to ethics has been an important trend in post-marxist social scientific approaches to the study of islam and muslim societies, with inspiration from talal asad's reading of michel foucault on the care and cultivation of the self. such attention to ethics and subject formation (for foucault, subjectivation) came in part as a critique of instrumentalist readings of subjects and agency, most notably, in work about islam and politics or political islam. at the same time, it was a response to simplistic understandings of religious practice within both the social sciences and more generally, understandings that tend to be informed by liberal models of social action that privilege 'individual' and 'autonomous' trajectories assumed to be moving toward presumed western models of emancipation or enlightenment, particularly in western feminism. the study of islam and muslim societies with a focus on ethics has been perhaps most fully developed by saba mahmood (2005) and charles hirschkind (2006), both of whom conducted research in cairo in the 1990s. given space limitations, we can only briefly point to some of the problems with the ethical turn in the study of islam (e.g. bangstad 2011; mittermaier 2012; deeb 2015; cf. fadil and fernando 2015; kloos and beckers 2017). some of this work tends to privilege micropolitics over politics and downplays '[d]ifferences in orientations, which might vary [sociologically] by social location or class' (soares and osella 2009: 10). at the same time, broader macropolitics are not sufficiently considered, the state and all of its mechanisms coercive, repressive, persuasive, disciplinary, and so forth are largely ignored. there is also a danger of cultural determinism in such totalising images of piety movements, focusing as they do almost exclusively on 'prescriptive discourses' and therefore on what many would consider 'orthodoxy' (ahmed 2016: 284, n. 84). as scholars such as magnus marsden (2005) and samuli schielke (2009) have demonstrated, ambivalences, multivocality and contingencies shape the lives and actions of ordinary muslims. indeed, 'struggle, ambivalence, incoherence, and failure must also receive attention in the study of everyday religiosity' (soares and osella 2009: 11). by shifting attention to the complexities of lived, everyday religion (otayek and soares 2007; soares and osella 2009; cf. marsden 2005), in this article we are not seeking either to resuscitate stale and altogether improbable oppositions between textual islam and a demotic, almost spontaneous religiosity (akin to orsi's 2002 reading of 'popular' catholicism), or to attribute degrees of authenticity and legitimacy to different or competing traditions of islamic orthopraxis, as some na ve critics such as fadil and fernando (2015; cf. ingram 2018: 211 12) have suggested. the latter privileges modalities of being muslim with ethical self-cultivation as central; this is at the expense of other ways of being muslim that are more diverse than the rather restricted sample of young european muslims studied in such recent sociological and anthropological research (e.g. fadil 2011; fernando 2016). such a narrow reading of contemporary islam and ways of being muslim, in which those who are committed to a pious lifestyle and salafis are conflated and privileged, is not only empirically flawed but misguided, not least for ignoring ways of being muslim in postcolonial settings beyond european contexts. in our understanding of lived, everyday religion rather than in fadil and fernando's misrepresentation of the latter we seek to develop an analytics of becoming and being muslim via intersectional exchanges and practices within the wider and thus political and contested fields of social and cultural production. this move does not privilege practice over theology, or vice versa, but rather underscores how ways of being muslim are crafted, imagined and experienced in relation to historical political and economic transformations which simultaneously constitute and transcend ethnic-religious boundaries, as well as those between secular and religious spheres. as such, the notion of lived religion points us towards appreciating the historical and contemporary circulation of practices, aesthetics and theologies, not only within and between religious traditions, but also across different social fields (see soares 2005; osella 2018). however, rather than attempting to establish lines of causation between social fields, in our understanding of lived, everyday religion we intend to draw out in time-honoured anthropological fashion the contingent historical milieus in which particular modalities of moral reasoning and practical action develop. in other words, rather than positing somewhat fixed muslim identities and subjectivities, the focus here is on historical modalities of being muslim in all their complexities, tensions and contradictions, which remain always inchoate and in the process of becoming. we will illustrate this in case studies from southwestern nigeria and south india, before returning to the implications of studying islam and muslim societies at the current historical juncture and religiosity more generally. our first case is from nigeria, a country whose population many characterise as almost evenly divided between muslims and christians. both british colonialism, beginning in the 19th century, and american christian missionary activities, since the era of the abolition of the slave trade (see sanneh 2001) and through the 20th century, have had a profound impact on lived religion and religiosity in nigeria. the long history of christian evangelism with strong american connections dating to the 19th century (shankar 2014) led not only to the spread of christianity in nigeria but also to the spread of modern forms of schooling, associational life and individualistic models of reform (reichmuth 1998), which both christians and muslims often adopted with alacrity, especially in southwestern nigeria. throughout the 20th century there were complex encounters between christians and muslims in a context where what has come to be called yoruba religion or african 'traditional' religion has been practised. since the 1980s, nigeria has witnessed the dramatic expansion of both muslim and christian proselytisation activities, which are often interrelated. both christian and muslim individuals, groups and associations in the country have sought greater transnational links for funding and support for their activities. however, determining which activities came first and who borrowed or appropriated methods, styles and techniques from whom will never be uncontroversial. stepped-up christian proselytising activities in nigeria can be clearly linked to the global christian resurgence witnessed throughout the world since the 1980s but also to the long history of christian evangelism in the country. beginning in the 1980s, nigerian protestants, including evangelical christians and pentecostals, along with euro-american missionaries, embarked on extensive evangelisation efforts, including some specifically directed toward muslims. from the perspective of many christian missionaries, the muslim areas of nigeria fall within so-called 'under-evangelised' areas of the world, and muslims became a favoured target. protestant missionaries actively employed a variety of techniques, such as open-air revivals (or 'crusades') and print and audio-visual materials (books, pamphlets, films, videos and audiocassettes) in their sometimes sophisticated (but frequently clumsy and aggressive) campaigns, to which many muslims have taken offence. outside funding and support for such activities particularly from north america have been key, and this is part of the larger context within which some of the conflict and violence between christians and muslims in the country since the 1980s must be understood (cf. falola 1998; kukah 2007). while christian activists in nigeria looked to north america for models, funding and support, many nigerian muslims looked to the presumed heartland of the muslim world. since the 1980s, petrodollars have been channelled into foreign aid, education and scholarships in many places in sub-saharan africa. although it is important not to exaggerate the influence of arab and muslim countries in sub-saharan africa, the longstanding rivalry between saudis and iranians in the wake of the iranian revolution has had lasting effects in nigeria. some young nigerian muslims eagerly looked to the iranian revolution for inspiration for the transformation of their own society at a time when the space for political debate was restricted. many also looked to saudi arabia and other arab countries for educational opportunities, funding possibilities and ideological/doctrinal backing in debates with other muslims (thurston 2016). saudi arabia provided considerable support to the country's leading muslim reformist intellectual, chief kadi abubakar gumi (d. 1992). gumi eventually articulated a harsh critique of sufi orders, which have long been important in nigeria, and his close followers went on to found the reformist muslim organisation, 'the society for the removal of innovation and reinstatement of tradition', better known by its hausa name, yan izala. perhaps one of the world's largest muslim reformist organisations, izala and its offshoots have espoused an austere version of islam and have certain affinities with saudi ways of being muslim (see umar 1993; loimeier 1997; kane 2003; last 2014). members of izala are frequently disdainful of both those muslims who do not embrace its vision and christians, and this has led to prolonged controversies and debates. izala and its offshoots also have a reputation for aggressive proselytising and the use of media to propagate their messages. while the saudis supported gumi and he actively sought to associate himself with the saudis, iran courted some of gumi's intellectual and political rivals, particularly ibrahim el zakzaky (b. 1953), the fiery activist from the muslim students society (mss) (founded in the 1950s), the muslim student organisation represented throughout the country. el zakzaky and his newer group called the muslim brothers have advocated an iranian-style islamic revolution and state as the solution to nigeria's problems (see mustapha and bunza 2014). as many nigerian muslims have emphasised during field research, saudi and iranian rivalry played itself out in nigeria, as both countries sought to influence and mobilise nigeria's often restless muslim youths. the effects of this rivalry can still be felt today. numerous nigerian muslims have subsequently converted to shi'a islam in northern nigeria and in recent years have sometimes faced persecution by the sunni muslim majority in the country and/or the nigerian state. such large-scale muslim organisations as izala, as well as the mss and later el zakzaky's muslim brothers have been important conduits for muslim activism and proselytising in nigeria. various elements have been radicalised since the 1980s, most notably maitatsine, subsequently the self-styled nigerian taliban and most recently boko haram. by the late 1980s and early 1990s, many muslim activists and groups were actively seeking to counter christian evangelisation efforts and to spread islam, and they attempted to do so with youthful, revolutionary fervour. and some christian youths matched muslim youths with their own fervour. following the south african muslim preacher ahmed deedat, young muslim activists began to practise what they called 'comparative religious studies'; what they meant by this was to educate themselves about christianity and the bible so as to be better equipped to argue with christians, with the ultimate goal of getting them to convert to islam (see larkin 2008). it goes without saying that many christians took offence at such efforts to debunk their religion and get them to convert to islam. since the 1980s, there has been considerable loss of life and destruction of homes, mosques and churches in nigeria that relates in part to some of these developments. other factors, including such political economic factors as migration, the struggle for resources, land and citizen rights, and national politics have also played important roles in various conflicts. in addition, it is important to underscore lingering late colonial-era tensions over the encounters between muslims and christians in the public sphere and more informal spheres in nigeria (e.g. barnes 2004). although muslims and christians sometimes seem to be at loggerheads, this is of course not always the case. however, the extension of sharia law to cover criminal law in 12 northern states beginning in the late 1990s seemed to take this to a new level. the fact that 12 muslim-majority states within nigeria's ostensibly secular federal state system had taken such a step led to considerable debate about the nature of the state, secularity and christian muslim relations. the climate of competing title: when sects become middle class: impression management among middle-class pentecostals in argentina
display_name: When Sects Become Middle Class: Impression Management among Middle-Class Pentecostals in Argentina
abstract: sect-to-church theory assumes that sects will become more church-like as members socioeconomic status improves. by abandoning tension-related characteristics, they decrease the level of tension with their social environment. studying pentecostal middle-class congregations in argentina, this article shows that the reduction of tension involves impression management: the studied middle-class congregations display middle-class features (e.g., educational training) and selectively shield tension-related practices (e.g., glossolalia) from the glances of non-pentecostal peers. instead of abandoning tension-related practices to reduce tension, middle-class congregations strategically adjust their religious practices depending on the extent to which these are accessible for relevant outsiders, switching between sect-like and church-like styles of religion.

title: the vatican anti-gender theory and sexual politics: an african response
display_name: The Vatican Anti-Gender Theory and Sexual Politics: An African Response
abstract: pope francis did not only speak at the pontifical council for the family's world meeting of families in philadelphia, but also met with a gay couple (one of them was his former student) in washington dc (yardley and goodstein 2015).but as the new york times reported, the pontiff also privately met with kim davis (a us county clerk in kentucky, who refused to issue marriage licenses to same-sex couples despite the court order).in november 2015, pope francis toured africa.despite the growing demonization of, and violence directed on sexual minorities, the pontiff did not utter a word on sexuality during his tour of the continent.yet his visit followed the 2014 african commission on human and peoples' rights resolution to protect sexual minorities against 'acts of violence, discrimination and other human rights violations; corrective' rape, physical assaults, torture, murder, arbitrary arrests, detentions, extra-judicial killings and executions, forced disappearances, extortion and blackmail.'(2014: resolution 275).in june 2016, however, pope francis called on christians and the roman catholic church to ask for forgiveness from gays 'for the way they had treated them' (pullella 2016).the contradictory nature of pope francis's attitude to sexual minorities is arguably informed by the vatican's opposition to gender theory, which he once compared to nuclear weapons (mcelwee 2015).as cardinal bergoglio in argentina, pecheny, jones and ariza attest, pope francis described same-sex marriages as 'destructive pretension of god's plan' aimed at destroying god's image: man and woman.as pope, he reiterated this position in his address to the colloquium humanum in rome.organized around the paradigm of complementarity, diverse religious traditions and faiths affirmed complementarity as foundational to the future of the human family.

title: the positive confession movement and its influence and legacy on the neo-charismatic movement
display_name: The Positive Confession Movement and its influence and legacy on the Neo-Charismatic Movement
abstract: this article focuses on one of the branches of charismatic movement known as positive confession or word of faith movement. the movement is called with some other names due to its emphasis on faith confession or claiming by faith whatever one needs, especially in areas of wealth and health. the fundamental message of the movement is that a believer has the power or authority to unshackle himself from sickness, poverty, or any negative circumstances that may steal away happiness and peace. the intention is to trace its influence on the modern neocharismatic movement. to understand the movement fully, research has been done on its history, identity, message, dogma, and why its dogma is attractive to neo-charismatic movement. the basic reason for this african proclivity to positive confession movement is that africans look for the faith that can enhance their privileges and power. the tenets of faith for this movement are identified as its main distinctive, therefore making some impression that the movement is a credible alternative for people in poverty, seeking some way out this dire situation of lacking material goods. the conclusion captures some positives and weaknesses in the movement. an appeal is made for the movement to draw the balance between its prosperity gospel and the evangelical values of commitment, character, sacrifice, holiness, and contentment.

title: banker, pastor, teef : christian financial elites and vernaculars of accountability in ghana
display_name: Banker, pastor, teef: Christian financial elites and vernaculars of accountability in Ghana

authorships.name: Anna‐Riikka Kauppinen
institutions: Graduate Institute of International and Development Studies

abstract: abstract when nine ghanaian banks collapsed during the country's 2017 2019 financial crisis, a charismatic pentecostal pastor was at the center of public accusations as the board chairman of one of the failed banks. his role put a spotlight on the growing influence of charismatic pentecostal institutions and elites in ghana's financial market. shifting the perspective between diverse actors who reckoned with the bank's collapse, from ordinary christians to artist activists, this article explores how ghanaians evaluated the culpability of the pastor and in so doing problematized who christian elites involved in banking and business are accountable to: god, their congregants, or the public at large? we argue that global financial liberalization has generated new types of financial elites, pentecostal pastors among them, who become subject to new lines of accountability. holding someone accountable comes with stakes expressed through vernacular registers that demonstrate how financial markets are engulfed in broader social relations and regimes of ethical evaluation.

title: globalisation from below: conceptualising the role of the african diasporas in africa's development
display_name: Globalisation from below: conceptualising the role of the African diasporas in africa's development
abstract: in the past both african studies and development studies have ignored questions of the african diaspora. this point was made by zack williams back in 1995 but since then there has not been much work attempting to rectify this matter. in this article we put forward a framework for examining the role of diaspora in development. this centres on recognising that the formation of the african diaspora has been intimately linked to the evolution of a globalised and racialised capitalism. while the linkages between capitalism, imperialism and displacement are dynamic we should avoid a simplistic determinism that sees the movements of african people as some inevitable response to the mechanisms of broader structures. the complexity of displacement is such that human agency plays an essential role and avoids the unhelpful conclusion of seeing africans as victims. it is this interplay of structural forces and human agency that gives diasporas their shifting, convoluted and overlapping geometry. having established that we examine the implications of a diasporic perspective for understanding the development potential of both africans in diaspora and those who remain on the continent. we argue that both politically and economically the diaspora has an important part to play in contemporary social processes operating at an increasingly global scale. the key issues we address are embedded social networks in the diaspora, remittances and return, development organisations, religious networks, cultural dynamics, and political institutions. we conclude by suggesting where diasporic concerns will take us in the next few years.

title: the spirit world awareness in the new testament - a missiological challenge
display_name: The spirit world awareness in the New Testament - A missiological challenge
abstract: the idea of power concepts and power encounters is not strange to biblical revelation as it is often assumed. this impact of the invisible world onto the material world does not seem to have imposed a problem to the early readers of the new testament. the spirit world of the new testament, which is amazingly akin to the african situation (or third world), needs our theological appreciation for the modern day church to be in a position to effectively carry its missiological function in the world, especially in africa.

title: guess who's coming to church: the chicago defender , the federal council of churches, and rethinking shared faith in interracial religious practice
display_name: Guess Who's Coming to Church: The Chicago Defender, the Federal Council of Churches, and Rethinking Shared Faith in Interracial Religious Practice
abstract: abstract on the cover page of the september 23, 1922, issue of the chicago defender, editor robert s. abbott announced go-to-a-white-church sunday. less than a month later, the federal council of churches announced its inaugural race relations sunday. through a comparative analysis of these two events, this article reconsiders historians tendency to assume and emphasize a shared faith across racial lines when discussing interracial religious practice in various historical contexts. go-to-a-white-church sunday was intended both to introduce white churchgoers to black respectability and to provide moral guidance to white churchgoers, whose racism rendered their faith something other than true christianity. notwithstanding ceremonial nods to interracial religious brotherhood, abbott's campaign hinged more so on shared understandings of respectability than on shared christian faith. while the fcc's race relations sunday differed in its valorization of white christianity, with proclamations that interracial religious brotherhood was sufficient to solve the race problem, both events displayed a shared faith in the power of interracial proximity in itself to accomplish their respective ends. historians have replicated this problematic faith in interracial proximity by using language of racial transcendence and writing as if interracial religious practice is egalitarian unless proven otherwise. this article calls for more critical, contextually mindful approaches.

title: breaking the spirit of poverty in african pentecostal christianity
display_name: Breaking the Spirit of Poverty in African Pentecostal Christianity
abstract: abstract poverty is one of africa s most intractable problems. decades of deliberate and strategic socioeconomic policies have not yielded considerable concrete results to eradicate it. upon succeeding the brutal colonial administration, the burgeoning african governments promised their citizens material well-being through socioeconomic development. a half century later the continent is perpetually witnessing a blatant betrayal of dreams. just like the african governments that succeeded colonial governments, religious organizations continue to promise poverty eradication by divine means to their adherents, whose numbers keep exploding across the continent. the pentecostal variant of african christianity is particularly renowned for its promises of wealth, health, and prosperity through supernatural divine power: in the bible, god has promised to deliver immense material goods to those who believe in jesus christ. the expediency of these promises to alleviate poverty and bring about social transformation is debatable. some scholars argue that african pentecostalism is an elaborately complex increase in religious activities devoid of social structural transformation, while others opine that it contributes positively to development. in asking whether african pentecostal christianity is a move toward or a distraction from development, this article broadly explores discourses on pentecostalism and development in africa. arguably, in the endeavor to preach and live out the experiential power of the holy spirit, pentecostal christianity in africa inadvertently plays a role in the broader ongoing development discourse. although they do not view themselves as religious or religion , pentecostal churches attempts to make the teachings of jesus christ relevant to the mundane help individual believers cope with life s stresses and vulnerabilities. however, it does not transform the social conditions that create problems for individuals. the liberating hope of african pentecostal christianity lies in theologically nuancing its discourses to meaningfully engage in global development discourses.

title: pentecostalism as a theological tradition
display_name: Pentecostalism as a Theological Tradition
abstract: abstract the concern for a theological tradition among pentecostals responds to pressing questions of the recognition, invention, and rejection of tradition in late modern society and religion. tradition, to put it succinctly, is a concern not for the past but for the future of pentecostalism. this essay critically examines the challenges of designating pentecostal theology as a global tradition by asking what theological elements constitute pentecostalism as a tradition, what are the dominant theological patterns of its reenactment, and how these constructs aid or resist the formation of pentecostal theology in the future. the quest for answers follows the five essential patterns of tradition proposed by anthony giddens: collective memory, ritual expression, a formulaic conception of truth, guardians of the tradition, and its normative content. the results form an ideological, historical, and institutional critique of pentecostalism and its existential challenges as a theological tradition.

title: decolonising the commercialisation and commodification of the university and theological education in south africa
display_name: Decolonising the commercialisation and commodification of the university and theological education in South Africa
abstract: this article problematises the critical subject of the decolonisation of the university and theological education in south africa from the neo-colonisation of commercialisation and commodification. the article, written from a decolonial perspective, serves as an epistemic critique of the cultures of corporatisation, rationalisation and entrepreneurship in higher education driven by the marketisation of society by the neoliberal institutions of globalisation. the article engages the role of decolonising theological education by drawing insights from african/black theologies, the discourse on africanisation and liberation to counter the strangulation and dominance of the commodification and commercialisation of theological education and prosperity theology in africa, particularly in south africa.
